executiveSummary: Chapter 2 establishes the IASB's Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting as the theoretical foundation underlying all accounting standards, organized across three levels: the objective of financial reporting, the qualitative characteristics and elements of financial statements, and the recognition, measurement, and disclosure concepts. The framework concludes that useful financial information must be relevant and faithfully represented, and that companies apply accrual-basis accounting guided by the measurement, revenue recognition, expense recognition, and full disclosure principles to faithfully report economic reality.
keyTopics: Purpose and Need for a Conceptual Framework: A conceptual framework is a coherent system of concepts flowing from an objective; without it, standard-setting devolves into personal, inconsistent judgments. The IASB's 2018 Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting comprises eight chapters covering the objective through capital maintenance.

Objective of Financial Reporting: The primary objective is to provide financial information useful to present and potential equity investors, lenders, and other creditors in making resource-allocation decisions. Management stewardship—how well management uses company resources—is also explicitly part of this objective under the 2018 update.

Fundamental Qualitative Characteristics: Relevance (predictive value, confirmatory value, materiality) and faithful representation (completeness, neutrality, freedom from error) are the two qualities that make information decision-useful. Neither characteristic alone is sufficient; both must be present for information to be genuinely useful.

Enhancing Qualitative Characteristics: Comparability (including consistency across periods), verifiability, timeliness, and understandability complement the fundamental qualities without substituting for them. The cost constraint—benefits must exceed costs—is the pervasive limitation on all reporting.

Elements of Financial Statements: The Conceptual Framework defines five elements: assets (present economic resource controlled as a result of past events), liabilities (present obligation to transfer an economic resource), equity (residual interest), income (increases in equity from non-owner sources), and expenses (decreases in equity from non-owner sources). These elements articulate across statements so that period-of-time elements drive changes in moment-in-time elements.

Basic Accounting Assumptions: Five assumptions underpin financial accounting: economic entity (company activity is separate from owners), going concern (entity will continue indefinitely), monetary unit (money is a stable common denominator), periodicity (activities can be divided into artificial time periods), and accrual basis (events are recorded when they occur, not when cash changes hands).

Measurement Principles—Historical Cost vs. Current Value: IFRS employs a mixed-attribute system; historical cost provides verifiability and faithfulness at acquisition, while current value bases (fair value, value in use/fulfillment value, current cost) provide greater relevance for certain assets and liabilities. Fair value is defined as the exit price in an orderly market transaction and is organized into a three-level hierarchy from quoted prices (Level 1) to unobservable inputs (Level 3).

Revenue and Expense Recognition Principles: Revenue is recognized when a performance obligation is satisfied, following a five-step model; expenses are recognized by matching efforts to revenues (product costs) or immediate period charge-off (period costs). The full disclosure principle requires that all information material to informed decision-making appear in the financial statements, notes, or supplementary information.

importantDefinitions.Conceptual Framework: A coherent system of interrelated concepts that flows from an objective and provides guidance on identifying, recognizing, measuring, and reporting financial information.
importantDefinitions.Relevance: The quality of financial information that is capable of making a difference in a decision because it has predictive value, confirmatory value, or both.
importantDefinitions.Materiality: A company-specific threshold of relevance whereby omitting or misstating an item could influence the decisions of users; assessed on both quantitative magnitude and qualitative nature.
importantDefinitions.Faithful Representation: The quality that ensures reported numbers and descriptions match what really existed or happened; requires completeness, neutrality, and freedom from material error.
importantDefinitions.Prudence: The exercise of caution when making judgments under uncertainty so that assets and income are not overstated and liabilities and expenses are not understated; reintroduced in the 2018 Conceptual Framework as supportive of neutrality.
importantDefinitions.Going Concern Assumption: The presumption that a company will continue to operate long enough to fulfill its objectives, justifying historical cost accounting and depreciation policies.
importantDefinitions.Accrual Basis of Accounting: The method under which transactions are recorded in the periods in which economic events occur, regardless of when cash is received or paid; required under IFRS.
importantDefinitions.Historical Cost Principle: The measurement approach that records assets and liabilities at the amount paid or agreed upon at the date of acquisition, providing a verifiable and faithful benchmark.
importantDefinitions.Fair Value: The price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date; a market-based, exit-value measure.
importantDefinitions.Performance Obligation: A promise in a contract with a customer to transfer a distinct good or service; revenue is recognized when (or as) this obligation is satisfied.
importantDefinitions.Full Disclosure Principle: The practice of providing all information of sufficient importance to influence the judgment of an informed user, presented in financial statements, notes, or supplementary disclosures.
importantDefinitions.Cost Constraint: The pervasive limitation that the costs of providing financial information must not exceed the benefits derived from its use.

accountingTreatments: Revenue recognition—performance obligation satisfied: Record revenue in the period the performance obligation is met, not when cash is received. Example journal entry when Klinke Cleaners performs service on June 30 but collects in July: Dr. Accounts Receivable / Cr. Service Revenue on June 30; Dr. Cash / Cr. Accounts Receivable in July.

Expense recognition—matching principle (product costs): Costs directly tied to generating revenue (materials, labor, overhead) are capitalized and expensed in the same period as the related revenue, not when cash is paid. Example: Dr. Inventory (or Work-in-Process) / Cr. Cash or Payables when incurred; Dr. Cost of Goods Sold / Cr. Inventory when revenue is recognized.

Expense recognition—period costs: Administrative costs with no direct revenue linkage (officers' salaries, general overhead) are expensed immediately in the period incurred. Example: Dr. Salaries Expense / Cr. Salaries Payable.

Historical cost measurement of assets: Assets are recorded at acquisition cost and carried at that cost less accumulated depreciation/amortization; price-level changes are ignored under the monetary unit assumption. Example: Equipment purchased for $500,000: Dr. Equipment $500,000 / Cr. Cash $500,000.

Fair value re-measurement (current value): When IFRS requires or permits fair value, assets (e.g., financial instruments, investment properties) are re-measured at each reporting date. A decline in fair value: Dr. Impairment Loss / Cr. Asset (or Fair Value Adjustment), while an increase: Dr. Asset / Cr. Other Comprehensive Income or Gain.

Full disclosure in notes: Items that meet element definitions but are not recognized (e.g., contingent liabilities due to measurement uncertainty) must be disclosed in the notes. No debit/credit entry is made for unrecognized contingencies; instead, qualitative and quantitative narrative disclosure is required.
criticalFormulas: Accounting Equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Variables: Assets = economic resources controlled; Liabilities = present obligations; Equity = residual interest. Numerical example: If Assets = $500,000 and Liabilities = $200,000, then Equity = $300,000.

Materiality Rule of Thumb: Item Amount / Net Income >= 5% suggests potential materiality. Variables: Item Amount = amount of unusual or separately disclosed item; Net Income = income from operations for the period. Numerical example (Illustration 2.3, Company B): $5,000 / $10,000 = 50%, clearly material; Company A: $20,000 / $1,000,000 = 2%, likely immaterial.

Revenue Recognition Amount (five-step model): Revenue Recognized = Transaction Price Allocated to Satisfied Performance Obligation(s). Variables: Transaction Price = total consideration expected; Allocated portion = amount assigned to the specific obligation satisfied. Numerical example: Airbus signs a €100 million contract; upon delivery of aircraft satisfying one performance obligation, it recognizes €100 million (assuming a single obligation).

Depreciation—Straight-Line (referenced in Practice Problem): Annual Depreciation = (Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life. Numerical example from Practice Problem: Warehouse cost £1,000,000, residual value £0, life 10 years: Annual depreciation = £1,000,000 / 10 = £100,000 (controller improperly doubled this to £200,000 to reflect replacement cost, which is not permitted under historical cost principle).
illustrativeExample: Klinke Cleaners—Revenue Recognition (Chapter text, p. 1003–1007): Klinke performs dry-cleaning services on June 30 (satisfies the performance obligation) but does not collect cash until the first week of July. Under the accrual basis and revenue recognition principle, Klinke records on June 30: Dr. Accounts Receivable $X / Cr. Service Revenue $X. When cash is collected in July: Dr. Cash $X / Cr. Accounts Receivable $X. If Klinke had incorrectly used the cash basis, no revenue would appear in June, understating June income and overstating July income—a violation of IFRS. Additionally, the Practice Problem (Meadow plc, item 4) illustrates that land purchased for £320,000 and improved for £80,000 cannot recognize £180,000 of revenue based on an appraisal when no sale has occurred, because the performance obligation (transfer of land to buyer) has not been satisfied.
disclosurePresentationNotes: Fair value hierarchy disclosure: Companies must disclose the fair value measurement amount and the hierarchy level (Level 1, 2, or 3) for each major group of assets and liabilities measured at fair value; Level 3 measurements require additional disclosure about the valuation process and significant unobservable inputs.

Accounting policy changes (consistency): When a company switches accounting methods (e.g., inventory valuation from FIFO to average cost), the nature and effect of the change and its justification must be disclosed in the financial statements for the period of change; the auditor's report will also reference the change in an explanatory paragraph.

Contingencies and uncertainties not recognized on the face of statements: Items that meet element definitions but cannot be reliably measured—or whose existence is uncertain—are disclosed in the notes to financial statements with qualitative description and, where possible, quantitative ranges.

Supplementary information: Information of high relevance but lower reliability (e.g., oil and gas companies' proven reserve estimates and discounted cash flows) is presented as supplementary data outside the primary financial statements to provide additional decision-useful context without distorting recognized amounts.
potentialPitfalls: Confusing prudence with aggressive conservatism: Prudence under the 2018 Conceptual Framework means cautious judgment under uncertainty, not a license to systematically understate assets or overstate liabilities. Deliberate understatement in one period inflates income in future periods, violating neutrality and producing results that are neither prudent nor faithfully representative.

Recognizing revenue or gains before a performance obligation is satisfied: As illustrated by the Meadow plc land example, companies sometimes recognize revenue based on appreciation in value (appraisal gains) rather than on transfer of the good or service. Under IFRS, revenue is only recognized when the performance obligation is satisfied—not when market value increases—so recording unrealized gains as revenue is a direct violation of the revenue recognition principle.

Applying the cost constraint or materiality as a blanket excuse to omit information: Materiality is both quantitative and qualitative; items below a 5% net income threshold may still be material if they convert a loss to a profit, mask an illegal transaction, or affect management compensation. Similarly, the cost constraint does not justify omitting disclosures when the benefits to users clearly exceed preparation costs, and disclosure in notes is never a substitute for correct accounting treatment on the face of the statements.

sources: Learning Objective 1 (lines 95–221): Describes the usefulness of a conceptual framework, the development of the 2018 IASB Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting (eight chapters), and the objective of general-purpose financial reporting.

Learning Objective 2 (lines 267–686): Identifies the fundamental qualitative characteristics (relevance, faithful representation), enhancing characteristics (comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability), cost constraint, and the five basic elements of financial statements.

Learning Objectives 3 and 4 (lines 687–1191): Reviews the five basic accounting assumptions (economic entity, going concern, monetary unit, periodicity, accrual basis) and explains the four basic principles (measurement/historical cost and current value, revenue recognition, expense recognition, full disclosure) and the cost constraint.
